title: The 1929 Deed in Which Spedan Lewis Signed Away His Profits
dek: In April 1929 John Spedan Lewis put his London shops in trust for their staff, gave up their income and kept control for another 21 years.

story.event: Signing the First Trust Settlement, putting the family stores in trust for their employees
story.summary: On 18 April 1929, a year after inheriting both of his father's London stores, John Spedan Lewis signed the First Trust Settlement, transferring his shares in John Lewis, Peter Jones and the Odney Estate to trustees for the employees and creating the John Lewis Partnership. He took bonds and no further income from the business but kept practical control until the Second Trust Settlement of 26 April 1950 passed it to the trustees.
paragraphs: John Spedan Lewis started work in his father's drapery shop on Oxford Street, London, on his nineteenth birthday in 1904. At 21 he was given a quarter share, valued at £50,000. What troubled him, he later wrote in his book Partnership for All, was a sum: his father, his brother and he drew £26,000 a year from the business, while everyone else, people giving it "the whole of their working lives", shared about £16,000. He thought it unfair and inefficient.

His father opposed the idea of sharing the profits. A riding accident, two operations and a long recovery gave Spedan time to think it through. In 1914 his father let him run Peter Jones, a second and struggling shop in Sloane Square. Spedan cut an hour from the working day, paid departments commission and met elected staff representatives without their managers present. After a serious quarrel in 1916 he swapped his share of Oxford Street for control of Peter Jones, and in 1920 its outside shareholders approved a profit-sharing scheme. That April the staff magazine began calling employees Partners.

Father and son were reconciled after Spedan's mother died in 1924. In 1926 he took over his brother Oswald's share of Oxford Street, and when John Lewis died in 1928, aged 92, Spedan owned both stores outright. The whole income was now his to keep. On 18 April 1929 he signed the First Trust Settlement instead, transferring his shares in John Lewis, Peter Jones and the Odney Estate to trustees for the Partners; John Lewis Partnership Limited was incorporated five days later. In return, by the Partnership's own account, he was to receive bonds worth £1 million over 30 years, and he took no further income from the business.

What he kept was control. The settlement left him in complete practical charge, and he used it firmly: his Guardian obituary recalled him using the staff magazine to press strong views on how things should be done. Only on 26 April 1950 did a Second Trust Settlement pass his remaining shares and ultimate control to the trustees. Enid Lockett, a lawyer who helped shape it, told the Partnership's council that the chairman had "received not one penny" for this second gift. He died in 1963, aged 77.

quote.text: those are thought to be more liberal who have not made their wealth but inherited it; for in the first place they have no experience of want, and secondly all men are fonder of their own productions, as are parents and poets.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle thought heirs give more easily, having never known want. Spedan Lewis was giving away a business he had inherited, and he kept control of it for 21 more years. Neither fact makes the gift smaller, but both make it harder to call it simple.

reflection: What moved Spedan Lewis was a sum, not a slogan: three people drawing more than everyone else together. He did not hand everything over at once. He gave away the income first and kept the steering for another two decades, which some would call prudence and others reluctance.

You may one day have people beside you whose effort is not yet matched by what they receive, at work or at home. It helps to do the sum early, while it is small, and to be honest with yourself about which parts you are ready to share and which you are still holding, and why.
invitation: Think of one person whose work quietly holds yours up this month. Before the day ends, tell them plainly one specific thing they did that made your own work possible.

cross_checks.claim: Spedan Lewis judged that his family drew more from the business than all its other workers together (£26,000 against £16,000 a year, by his own account)
A profit-sharing scheme began at Peter Jones in 1920
On his father's death in 1928 Spedan Lewis became sole owner of the business

research_notes: The income figures come from the Guardian's 1963 obituary, which quotes Partnership for All (1948): £26,000 a year to father, brother and Spedan against £16,000 for everyone else. The Partnership's own history says only that the family received more than all employees together, while some later summaries (Wikipedia, London Remembers) say the amounts were equal; the story gives his own figures, attributed to his book. Profit-sharing date: the Partnership, the Guardian obituary and the Portsmouth case all give 1920; BBC News (2002) says he made good his pledge in 1919. The story uses 1920. Oswald's share: the Partnership's history says Oswald gave it to Spedan in 1926, while Wikipedia (citing Peter Cox's 2010 history) says Spedan bought it with a bank loan, so the story says neutrally that he took it over. The £1 million in bonds over 30 years and 'no further income' rest on the Partnership's own history and are attributed to it; Wikipedia describes the same arrangement as non-interest-bearing loan stock repaid over 30 years. The Partnership's online Memory Store pages on the trust settlements return 403 to automated requests and the Internet Archive was unreachable, so the Partnership's careers-site history (same archive material) and its corporate heritage page are cited instead. Enid Lockett's 'not one penny' refers to the 1950 settlement, not 1929, and the story says so. Aristotle's remark on heirs comes from his discussion of liberality and is applied by analogy; it is not a judgement Aristotle made of anyone in particular.
